issues.subcategory: Contradictory Bayes factor interpretation in Table 4
issues.description: The text states that non-illusory error rates increased with memory delay and reports BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay, but Table 4 reports the opposite: P(incl|data)=0.087, P(excl|data)=0.913, and BFincl=0.064 for Memory Delay, which is strong evidence against including Memory Delay under the authors' own interpretation scheme. Conversely, Table 4 reports BFincl=39110.895 for Target Type, while the text says only Memory Delay was relevant and that the increase was the same for pseudo- and real-letter targets. This is a serious internal/statistical inconsistency that directly affects the interpretation of Experiment 2 follow-up analyses.
issues.quote: For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42, see Appendix 1 for a full model comparison and Table 4 for an overview of BFincl for each model component).  Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) but this increase was the same for pseudo- and real letter targets (2% increase, from 10 to 12%, in both real and pseudo-letter targets).

issues.subcategory: Table 4 values conflict with narrative conclusions
issues.description: The narrative conclusion that target type does not affect other errors conflicts with Table 4, which shows overwhelming evidence for Target Type (BFincl=39110.895). If Table 4 is correct, the claim that non-illusory error rates were the same for real and pseudo-letter targets is unsupported. If the text is correct, the table contains substantial reporting errors. Either way, readers cannot evaluate the analysis.

issues.subcategory: Short-delay timing inconsistent across sections
issues.description: The manuscript inconsistently describes the short memory probe timing as 0.75 s, 0.5 s, and 500 ms. Experiment 1 used a 0.75 s delay, Experiment 2 describes a 0.5 s delay before the cue, and Experiment 4 uses 500 ms, yet the general discussion collapses these as if they were identical. This matters because the central claim depends on the temporal evolution of errors over hundreds of milliseconds to seconds.
issues.quote: Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2)

issues.subcategory: Experiment 4 figure numbering error
issues.description: Experiment 4 results refer to Figure 5, but the displayed figure is Figure 6. This impairs traceability of results and suggests inadequate proofreading/reporting consistency.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials.

issues.subcategory: Large post hoc participant exclusion based on confidence/trial counts
issues.description: Across experiments, many participants were excluded after data collection because they had too few high-confidence trials in one or more cells. This exclusion criterion removes participants who are less confident or perform differently and may bias estimates of high-confidence illusion rates. The exclusion is especially severe in Experiment 1 (17/40 excluded after training) and Experiment 2 (92/290 excluded). The manuscript does not justify the threshold statistically, report whether it was preregistered, or provide primary analyses including all participants with appropriate trial-level modeling.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded)

issues.subcategory: High exclusion/attrition not adequately addressed
issues.description: The exclusion rates are substantial, particularly 42.5% of Experiment 1 analyzed participants after training and 31.7% in Experiment 2. Excluded participants had far fewer high-confidence trials, meaning exclusions are related to the outcome-defining construct. The manuscript reports excluded participants' confidence rates but does not examine whether conclusions hold under alternative missing-data/exclusion approaches, creating risk of biased estimates and limited generalizability to less confident participants.
issues.quote: Included participants had on average 49.2% high confidence trial over all conditions ... Excluded participants had on average 15.7% high confidence trials over all conditions

issues.subcategory: Training-based selection limits Experiment 1 sample and comparability
issues.description: Experiment 1 required participants to pass extensive training on a different visual memory task, excluding 5 of 45 before the main task. Experiments 2–4 did not use this training. This creates sample-selection differences across experiments and may affect confidence, strategy use, and memory performance, yet the authors treat experiments as directly comparable replications.
issues.quote: Participants could only participate in the actual experiment, if they scored higher than 75% correct ... Since only 10% of participants were excluded from participating in the main experiment based on the training scores, the training procedure was not part of Experiments 2, 3 and 4

issues.subcategory: High confidence equated with false memory/illusion
issues.description: The core construct of 'illusory memory' is operationalized as high-confidence selection of the mirrored counterpart. High confidence, however, does not establish that participants experienced a false memory rather than made a confident response based on familiarity, decisional bias, metacognitive miscalibration, response mapping confusion, or task-induced category bias. The manuscript acknowledges response bias but tests it only indirectly and incompletely. This construct-validity issue affects the central claim.
issues.quote: Illusory memories should result in high confidence erroneous responses, where the participants has access to a memory trace (albeit an incorrect memory trace).

issues.subcategory: Increase over delay does not uniquely identify memory transformation
issues.description: The authors infer that increased errors over time must reflect transformation of correctly encoded percepts into illusory memories. However, delay effects can arise from differential forgetting of orientation information, response bias under uncertainty, retrieval-stage reconstruction, interference from the response display, or metacognitive changes. The design shows temporal dependence but does not isolate a specific causal mechanism of memory representations being 'converted'.
issues.quote: This effect must be due to processes ongoing in STM: Had these illusory memories been the result of changes in perception, they should have been present at the earlier probe as well.

issues.subcategory: Perception/encoding errors not ruled out
issues.description: The claim that delay-related increases rule out perceptual or encoding errors is overstated. A constant baseline of perceptual/encoding confusion plus increasing loss of diagnostic orientation information could produce the observed pattern without requiring initially correct percepts to be transformed. The early probe is not an immediate perceptual report and still occurs after a delay, masking, cueing, and later response selection processes.
issues.quote: To rule out that these errors reflect a perceptual error that has directly been encoded into STM, we test whether illusory responses increase over time

issues.subcategory: Response display may induce recognition/choice bias
issues.description: The task requires selecting among response options, often including the real counterpart and pseudo counterpart. The response display itself can bias decisions toward familiar real letters or create confusion at retrieval. Although Experiment 2 includes both target and counterpart, this does not eliminate familiarity or decisional biases. A production response, signal-detection design, or independent bias assessment would be needed to distinguish memory content from response choice bias.
issues.quote: The response screen consisted of 6 letters, 3 real letters and their pseudo counterparts.

issues.subcategory: Percentages based on conditional high-confidence trials may be misleading
issues.description: Error rates are calculated only among high-confidence trials, and participants with few high-confidence trials are excluded. Because confidence itself may vary by target type, delay, and error type, conditioning on confidence can induce selection/collider bias. The manuscript does not report the denominator for each condition, nor analyze confidence and accuracy jointly, so differences in 'high-confidence error rates' may reflect changes in confidence use rather than memory illusions.
issues.quote: Figure 2 shows the illusory and other error rates in high confidence trials.

issues.subcategory: No trial-level denominators/cell counts reported
issues.description: The manuscript reports percentages but not the number of critical trials contributing to each cell after exclusions, nor cell-specific high-confidence counts. This is essential because exclusion was based on low cell counts and because some conditions, especially pseudo-letter critical trials, may have relatively few observations per participant.
issues.quote: Together, the critical trials made up ~220 trials, 26% of all trials in the experiment.

issues.subcategory: Pre-registration absent and analytic decisions appear flexible
issues.description: The paper reports multiple experiments, exclusions, confidence filtering, Bayesian ANOVAs, follow-up ANOVAs, follow-up t-tests, collapsing over conditions after null effects, and sequential stopping in later experiments, but no preregistration or analysis plan is reported. This creates substantial researcher degrees of freedom, especially given the central reliance on high-confidence subsets and post hoc exclusions.
issues.quote: Since this analysis showed no effects of cue colour (see Results), the rest of the analysis was conducted while collapsing over the two cue colour conditions.

issues.subcategory: Sequential Bayes factor stopping insufficiently specified
issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 used ongoing sequential analyses with stopping when BF crossed 10, but critical details are missing: exact prior for the t-test, whether two-sided or directional, maximum sample size, minimum sample size, timing and number of looks, whether stopping rule was preregistered, and whether all analyses respect the sequential design. Optional stopping with Bayes factors can be valid under specified priors, but incomplete reporting prevents evaluation.
issues.quote: Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.

issues.subcategory: Sequential stopping based on t-test but main inference uses ANOVA
issues.description: The stopping rule in Experiments 3 and 4 was based on 'the critical t-test' comparing the effect of Error-Type for Real and Pseudo-letter targets, while reported primary analyses are Bayesian repeated-measures ANOVAs. Stopping on one analysis and reporting another can distort evidential interpretation unless fully planned and justified.
issues.quote: Sample size was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test, namely the comparison between the effect of Error-Type for Real and Pseudo-letter targets.

issues.subcategory: Bayesian ANOVA priors not specified
issues.description: The manuscript reports Bayes factors from JASP but does not specify the prior distributions/model priors beyond inclusion probabilities in tables. Bayes factors are prior-sensitive, especially for interactions. Replication and interpretation require reporting default prior settings, scale parameters, model prior structure, and whether effects obeyed heredity constraints.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4

issues.subcategory: Ambiguous or incorrect interpretation of BFm and BFincl
issues.description: The authors describe BFm as comparing posterior odds of models to 'prior explanatory value,' but model Bayes factors and inclusion Bayes factors have distinct meanings and depend on model prior odds. Some interpretations treat anecdotal evidence as support for hypotheses. In Experiment 1, the key Memory Delay × Error Type interaction has BFincl=4.21, only 'substantial' by their convention but modest, yet is used to support a strong mechanistic conclusion.
issues.quote: The interaction between Error Type and Memory Delay, (BFincl = 4.21) shows support for hypothesis 2

issues.subcategory: Anecdotal evidence overinterpreted for three-way pattern
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the authors describe condition-specific increases for pseudo-letter targets despite only anecdotal evidence for the relevant three-way interaction. Interpreting these subgroup patterns risks overstatement and selective emphasis.
issues.quote: Finally, there is only anecdotal evidence for a three-way interaction between Target Type, Error Type and Memory Delay (BFincl = 2.45): For pseudo-letter targets, illusory errors increase 12%

issues.subcategory: Follow-up tests after Bayesian model selection not fully reported
issues.description: Several follow-up t-tests are reported only as BF values without specifying paired/one-sample structure, priors, tails, exact contrasts, means/SDs/credible intervals, or correction/modeling strategy. This limits interpretability and replication.
issues.quote: going from 7% illusions for real-letter targets to 26% illusions for pseudo-letter targets: BF>1000 in a follow-up t-test

issues.subcategory: Online data collection in Experiment 4 lacks display/timing control
issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online on participants' own laptops via Neurotask/Zoom. Precise stimulus duration and timing are central to the study, but the manuscript does not report hardware/browser constraints, refresh-rate checks, exclusion for timing failures, viewing distance, screen size, visual angle calibration, or environmental controls. This is especially problematic for 250 ms displays and 500 ms delay conditions.
issues.quote: the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting . Participants ... started on their own laptop.

issues.subcategory: Visual angle calibration impossible/unclear for online experiment
issues.description: Stimuli are specified in degrees of visual angle in lab experiments, but Experiment 4 was online on participants' own laptops with no reported viewing-distance or screen-size calibration. Thus the actual stimulus sizes and eccentricities are unknown, affecting encoding difficulty and comparability to Experiments 2–3.
issues.quote: given the link to the Neurotask experiment, which they then started on their own laptop

issues.subcategory: Interference manipulation confounded with cue timing and display sequence
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the short-with-interference condition presents the irrelevant second display together with the cue, while other conditions present it later. This manipulation may affect attentional selection, cue visibility, retrieval, or response preparation, not just memory decay/interference. Therefore differences between short and short-with-interference cannot be attributed solely to STM deterioration.
issues.quote: If the probe appeared 0.75 seconds after memory display offset, it either appeared together with the irrelevant second display (the Short-with-interference condition), or it appeared in isolation (the Short condition).

issues.subcategory: Irrelevant second display may contaminate response/memory
issues.description: The 'irrelevant' display contains real and pseudo-letters and appears before the response. Even if unrelated, it can introduce proactive/retroactive interference, response priming, or source-confusion. The manuscript does not analyze whether letters in the second display overlapped with response options or influenced errors, nor whether illusion choices were present in the interference display.
issues.quote: To increase memory decay through task-irrelevant interference, a second display was included in each trial. This display consisted of randomly selected letters, unrelated to the memory display.

issues.subcategory: World knowledge confounded with stimulus familiarity and discriminability
issues.description: The authors interpret pseudo-to-real asymmetry as world knowledge, but real and mirrored letters differ in familiarity, nameability, verbal recoding, and possibly discriminability. These factors can affect encoding, maintenance, confidence, and response selection without requiring predictive world-knowledge-driven reshaping. The discussion acknowledges some alternatives but the experiments do not decisively separate them.
issues.quote: This suggests that world knowledge is a more important driver of illusory memories than visual similarity

issues.subcategory: Visual similarity argument oversimplified
issues.description: The manuscript argues visual similarity is identical in both directions because C and Ɔ are mirror counterparts. However, psychological similarity/discriminability need not be symmetric when one item is familiar/canonical and the other is unfamiliar/mirrored; category representations and orientation sensitivity can make confusability asymmetric. Thus the inference that asymmetry rules out similarity is too strong.
issues.quote: visual similarity between to-be-remembered target and the mirrored counterpart that is presented in the response screen is clearly identical in both cases.

issues.subcategory: No direct manipulation or measurement of lifelong letter priors
issues.description: The central construct 'world knowledge' is inferred from real-letter prevalence in everyday life, but individual differences in alphabet familiarity, reading fluency, native language/script, dyslexia, handedness/reading direction, or exposure to mirrored symbols are not measured. The sample is presumably Dutch psychology students but language background is not reported.
issues.quote: All experiments rely on the extensive experience participants have with the alphabet.

issues.subcategory: Student/psychology samples limit population claims
issues.description: Participants are mostly young university psychology students, often participating for course credit, with many women in some experiments. The manuscript makes broad claims about STM and memory generally without sufficiently limiting inference to young literate adults familiar with Latin letters.
issues.quote: The participants participated for student credits as part of a course within the first-year Psychology curriculum.

issues.subcategory: Stimulus-specific paradigm overgeneralized to STM broadly
issues.description: The conclusion that STM is shaped by expectations 'right from the formation of the first memory trace' is based on a highly specific task involving Latin letters and mirror reversals. Generalizing to all STM or visual percepts requires additional stimulus classes and tasks.
issues.quote: Thus, it seems that short-term memory is not always an accurate representation of what was just perceived. Instead, memory is shaped by what we expected to see, right from the formation of the first memory trace.

issues.subcategory: Randomization/counterbalancing insufficiently detailed
issues.description: The manuscript states that trial types were randomly intermixed, but does not specify counterbalancing of target identities, locations, pseudo-letter identities, response option positions, mapping of real/pseudo alternatives, or whether all letters appeared equally often as targets. These details are needed because letter identity and location could strongly influence mirror-confusion rates.
issues.quote: All conditions were randomly intermixed throughout the experiment.

issues.subcategory: Cue color manipulation in Experiment 2 may be ineffective/unlearned
issues.description: Experiment 2 attempts to test transiently induced expectations via cue color probabilities, but participants were apparently not informed of the contingency and post-experiment questionnaires did not reveal awareness. The manipulation may not have induced expectations at all, so the null result cannot support the conceptual conclusion that expectations need substantial time to develop.
issues.quote: The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses.

issues.subcategory: Unsupported conclusion from null cue-color effect
issues.description: The authors infer from no cue-color effect that expectations need substantial time to develop. A null effect in an implicit color-probability manipulation could instead reflect weak salience, insufficient learning, lack of awareness, color/luminance confounds, inadequate power for the interaction after exclusions, or inappropriate manipulation. The conclusion is speculative.
issues.quote: This is consistent with the notion that expectations need substantial time to develop before they can affect explicit, high confidence memories.

issues.subcategory: Cue colors differ in luminance
issues.description: The red and blue fixation/cue colors in Experiment 2 differ substantially in luminance (11.9 vs 6.47 cd/m2). If color cues affect attention or visibility, luminance differences could confound any cue-color effect or null interpretation. No counterbalancing of probability-color mapping is reported.
issues.quote: blue (CIE: 0.148, 0.078, luminance: 6.47 cd/m2) or red (CIE: 0.641, 0.341; luminance: 11.9 cd/m2).

issues.subcategory: No counterbalancing of color-probability mapping
issues.description: In Experiment 2, red always indicated lower pseudo-letter target probability and blue higher pseudo-letter target probability. Without counterbalancing across participants, any color-specific attention, salience, luminance, or learned association is confounded with probability condition.
issues.quote: If the fixation cross and the cue were red, a pseudo-letter was the target on 25% of the trials. The target was a pseudo-letter on 60% of the trials when the fixation cross and the cue were blue.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 probability imbalance conflicts with display composition
issues.description: Experiment 2 memory displays always include 2 pseudo-letters out of 6, yet the target is pseudo on 25% of red trials and 60% of blue trials. This requires nonuniform cueing conditional on color, but the manuscript does not describe how locations/targets were sampled or whether target locations/letter types were balanced. Without this, cue color may be confounded with cueing of particular positions or letters.
issues.quote: 2 of the 6 letters in the memory display were pseudo-letters... If the fixation cross and the cue were red, a pseudo-letter was the target on 25% of the trials. The target was a pseudo-letter on 60% of the trials when the fixation cross and the cue were blue.

issues.subcategory: Accuracy and confidence distributions incompletely reported
issues.description: Because the main outcome is high-confidence error, full accuracy, confidence distributions, calibration, and high-confidence correct rates by condition are necessary to interpret whether effects reflect memory distortion, changes in response criterion, or confidence use. The manuscript reports selected high-confidence error percentages but not complete response distributions.
issues.quote: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of four boxes (from 1-4, 1 = guess, 4 = certain).

issues.subcategory: Proportions analyzed with ANOVA despite bounded/non-normal data
issues.description: The analyses use repeated-measures ANOVAs on participant-level proportions. Proportions are bounded and may be based on unequal denominators across conditions, especially after high-confidence filtering. A hierarchical binomial/multinomial model would better account for trial counts, participant variability, and response categories. ANOVA on proportions can misestimate uncertainty.
issues.quote: error rates on high confidence trials were analyzed in an ANOVA with target type ... and relative occurrence of high confidence selection as the dependent variable.

issues.subcategory: Ignoring multinomial dependence among response categories
issues.description: Illusory errors, other errors, correct responses, and possibly 'none of these' are mutually exclusive response outcomes. Analyzing illusory and other error rates in ANOVA as if independent continuous measures does not model the multinomial structure and can obscure tradeoffs among categories.
issues.quote: the occurrence of illusory errors ... and other errors ... was calculated.

issues.subcategory: No effect-size uncertainty intervals
issues.description: The manuscript reports percentages and Bayes factors but no confidence/credible intervals or participant-level variability for main effects/interactions. This makes it difficult to assess precision and practical significance of effects, especially modest delay increases such as 4–5%.
issues.quote: Illusory responses increased from 14% to 19% in the longer delays

issues.subcategory: Feedback may alter strategies and response biases
issues.description: Participants received feedback after each trial or block and were repeatedly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters. Feedback may change strategies, confidence criteria, attention to mirror status, or learned base rates over the experiment. The manuscript does not analyze learning/fatigue/order effects despite long sessions with many trials.
issues.quote: After each trial the participant received feedback (correct/ incorrect response) on her performance.

issues.subcategory: No analysis of time-on-task or learning effects
issues.description: Given repeated feedback and hundreds of trials, participants may learn the base rates or change reliance on real-letter priors over time. The manuscript does not report block/order analyses, leaving open whether effects are stable STM illusions or task-learning artifacts.
issues.quote: The experiment consisted of 18 blocks of 25 trials.

issues.subcategory: Practice procedures differ across experiments
issues.description: Practice and training differ substantially across experiments: Experiment 1 includes extensive prerequisite training, Experiment 2 uses 12 practice trials with 2500 ms display, Experiment 3 uses gradually shortened displays, and Experiment 4 online practice via Zoom. These differences may affect encoding strategies and confidence, complicating comparisons across experiments.
issues.quote: Secondly, the display time for the memory display in practice trials was variable ... In each subsequent practice trial, the presentation of the memory display was shortened by 100 ms

issues.subcategory: Experiment 4 lacks explicit Methods heading
issues.description: Experiment 4 begins directly with Participants and does not clearly label a Methods section. While minor, it contributes to organizational ambiguity, especially because online methodological details are important.
issues.quote:
Experiment 4

Participants

issues.subcategory: Typographical/terminological inconsistency for pseudo-letter targets
issues.description: The manuscript sometimes refers to 'real-target letters' or 'mirrored targets' in ways that could confuse target identity with target category. This is minor but problematic in a design where target type and response type are central.
issues.quote: Each memory display and each response display consisted of equal numbers of pseudo- and real-target letters

issues.subcategory: Predictive processing account underdetermined by data
issues.description: The discussion presents predictive processing/Bayesian integration as a comfortable explanatory framework, but the experiments do not measure predictions, precision, prediction errors, or neural/computational quantities. The same data are compatible with familiarity-based retrieval, feature loss plus categorical reconstruction, verbal recoding, and response bias. The theoretical interpretation is plausible but overextended.
issues.quote: One possibility is that both perception and cognitive processes such as STM operate according to Bayesian principles.

issues.subcategory: Overstatement that FTT cannot explain findings
issues.description: The claim that fuzzy trace theory cannot account for the results rests on an assertion that high similarity should inhibit false memories, but the manuscript does not formally test FTT predictions in this paradigm and later acknowledges FTT-related verbal/gist mechanisms that could matter. The dismissal is stronger than warranted.
issues.quote: Therefore, it seems that FTT cannot accurately account for the occurrence of this type of memory illusions in STM.

issues.subcategory: Stimulus set/font not fully specified
issues.description: The exact font, letter rendering, size of letters, line thickness, anti-aliasing, and list of included asymmetric letters are not fully specified. For mirror-letter confusion, font and rendering can materially affect discriminability and replication.
issues.quote: Pseudo-letter were mirrored (i.e. flipped from left to right). Therefore only letters that changed when mirrored were included

issues.subcategory: Ethics/consent reporting incomplete for online data quality/privacy
issues.description: Experiment 4 used Zoom breakout rooms and screen sharing but does not describe online privacy safeguards, whether participants were monitored, whether screen sharing continued during the task, or how compliance/attention was verified. This affects both ethics and data-quality evaluation.
issues.quote: Via the share screen option, participants were given instructions and feedback during the practice block

issues.subcategory: No blinding of experimenter in online supervised practice
issues.description: The experimenter interacted with participants during practice in Experiment 4 and provided instructions/feedback via Zoom. The manuscript does not report standardized scripts or blinding to condition/progress. Although conditions are within-subject and computerized, differential instruction or assistance could influence performance.
issues.quote: participants were given instructions and feedback during the practice block

issues.subcategory: Unequal base rates complicate interpretation of Experiment 1 critical trials
issues.description: In Experiment 1, target type and availability of mirrored counterpart in the response display are deliberately unbalanced to make critical trials approximately equal. This creates complex base-rate and response-option contingencies that participants could learn, and makes raw pseudo-to-real versus real-to-pseudo comparisons difficult to interpret without a formal model of base rates and response options.
issues.quote: The target letter was a real letter in 75% of the trials and a pseudo-letter in the remaining 25%... If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half... only the real counterpart was one of the response options.

issues.subcategory: 'Other errors' may not be an appropriate baseline for illusions
issues.description: The authors compare mirrored-counterpart selections to selections of unrelated distractors and interpret higher mirrored selections as illusory memory. But the mirrored counterpart is uniquely related to the target by identity/name/shape, whereas unrelated distractors are not. Higher selection of the counterpart may reflect partial memory for identity with lost orientation, not a false memory of seeing the real letter. This baseline therefore does not cleanly distinguish illusion from partial-information errors.
issues.quote: hypothesis 1 - do illusions occur in STM? – by determining if participants confused pseudo-letter targets with their real counterpart with high confidence, or the other way around, more often than other high confidence errors

issues.subcategory: Partial identity memory confounded with orientation memory
issues.description: A participant may correctly remember the letter identity but forget or confuse mirror orientation, leading to selection of the mirrored counterpart. Calling this an 'illusory memory' of the counterpart may overstate the construct; the task does not separately measure memory for identity and orientation. The central effect could be an orientation-feature error biased toward canonical orientation.
issues.quote: Participants were instructed to report the letter that appeared at the cued location. They were explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters

issues.subcategory: Interference and time both treated as memory deterioration without direct memory-strength measure
issues.description: The manuscript assumes longer delay and interference reduce memory strength and uses this to infer increased reliance on priors. However, memory strength is not independently measured; changes in error patterns could reflect attentional capture, masking, or retrieval competition. The causal chain 'delay/interference → weaker memory trace → prior-driven illusion' remains inferential.
issues.quote: as memory deteriorates with a larger memory delay or more visual interference

issues.subcategory: No data/code availability statement
issues.description: The manuscript does not provide a data/code availability statement. Given complex exclusions, Bayesian analyses, and inconsistencies in reported tables, access to data and code is important for verification and replication.
issues.quote: The experiment was programmed in Matlab version 2012b using the Psychophysics Toolbox routines

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 Table 2 reports infinite Bayes factors without explanation
issues.description: Several BFincl values are reported as infinity in Table 2, likely due to numerical rounding where posterior exclusion probability is 0. The manuscript does not explain the numerical precision or whether these are exact/infinite or rounded. This matters for reproducibility and interpretation of Bayesian evidence.
issues.quote: Target Type | ... BFincl | ∞

issues.subcategory: Missing Appendix prevents verification of model comparisons
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly refers to Appendix 1 for full model comparisons, but the provided manuscript text does not include it. Without the appendix, readers cannot verify BFm values, alternative models, or model priors.
issues.quote: see Appendix 1 for full model comparison

issues.subcategory: No control using non-letter mirrored shapes
issues.description: The central claim is that alphabetic world knowledge drives pseudo-to-real memory illusions. A stronger design would include non-letter symbols or unfamiliar trained symbols with matched visual structure to isolate letter-specific priors from general mirror-orientation biases. The absence of such controls leaves construct ambiguity.
issues.quote: All experiments rely on the extensive experience participants have with the alphabet.

issues.subcategory: Claims about 'all memory stages' exceed tested intervals
issues.description: The abstract says findings support a view in which all memory stages, including STM, involve integration with predictions. The experiments test brief visual STM for letters over roughly 0.5/0.75 to 3 s, not all memory stages, all STM subsystems, or long-term memory mechanisms. This is an overgeneralization.
issues.quote: Our findings support a predictive processing view of the formation and maintenance of memory in which all memory stages, including STM, involve integration of bottom-up memory input with top-down predictions

issues.subcategory: Abstract says 1 or 2 seconds but experiments use up to 3 seconds
issues.description: The abstract frames the assumed accurate window as '1 or 2 seconds ago,' but the key long-delay evidence uses 3 seconds and some interference displays occur later. This is not fatal but imprecise given the temporal claims.
issues.quote: percepts formed just 1 or 2 seconds ago

issues.subcategory: Experiment 4 follow-up BF for 1% non-illusory increase presented as evidence despite small practical effect
issues.description: The non-illusory error increase from 6% to 7% is reported with BF=4.84, but no uncertainty intervals or exact model are provided. Given the large sample and many trials, statistically/Bayesian-supported tiny effects may not be practically meaningful; the manuscript uses this alongside a stronger illusion increase without clearly distinguishing magnitude from evidence.
issues.quote: the other non-illusory error rate only increased from 6% to 7% (BF = 4.84 in a follow up t-test).

issues.subcategory: Demographic imbalance not discussed
issues.description: Some experiments have strong gender imbalance (e.g., 51 women of 64 in Experiment 3) and all are young adults. The manuscript does not discuss whether demographic factors might affect letter familiarity, confidence, or generalizability.
issues.quote: 64 participants participated (51 women; age range 17-46 years, average age 20.5 years)

issues.subcategory: Potential motor/response-position biases not reported
issues.description: The response screen contains six options, but the manuscript does not specify whether option positions were randomized or counterbalanced. If real letters and pseudo-letters occupied systematic positions or if participants had spatial selection biases, error rates could be affected.
issues.quote: The response display consisted of 6 letters: the target letter ... two other randomly selected letters ... and 3 letters that did not appear

issues.subcategory: Confidence scale lacks validation/calibration
issues.description: The 1–4 confidence scale is central to defining memory illusions, yet no validation, calibration, or participant instruction details beyond labels are provided. 'Certain' may be used differently across participants and conditions; without calibration, high confidence does not necessarily correspond to subjective recollective experience.
issues.quote: then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4).

issues.subcategory: No masking control at stimulus offset
issues.description: The authors make claims about perception versus memory after brief displays, but do not use immediate post-stimulus masks to standardize iconic persistence or prevent continued processing after offset. Differences between short and long delays may include ongoing iconic/fragile visual processing rather than discrete STM storage.
issues.quote: On each trial the memory display was presented for 0.25 seconds. This was followed by a blank screen

issues.subcategory: Terminology conflates STM, WM, fragile memory, and report processes
issues.description: The manuscript discusses STM broadly but experiments use retro-cued multi-item visual memory tasks that may involve iconic, fragile, working memory, attention, and retrieval decision processes. The term 'STM illusions' may obscure which stage is affected, especially because cueing occurs after the display and response occurs after additional displays.
issues.quote: Here, we present 4 studies that explore whether STM in general is susceptible to false memories
